newsitem.title: JORDAN: British jet car seeks speed record in Jordan desert.
newsitem.headline: British jet car seeks speed record in Jordan desert.

text.p: Britain's jet car Thrust SSC arrived on Saturday in the deserts of southern Jordan for a planned assault on the world land speed record.

A giant Antonov transport plane flew the car to a military airbase near the parched mud flats of al-Jafr, where driver Andy Green will race it along a 10 mile (16 km) track in a bid to become the fastest man on four wheels.
"We have the capability to break the record," Green, a Royal Air Force pilot, told reporters before the car was hoisted out onto a moonlit runway.

But Green and Thrust designer Richard Noble, who set the existing record of 633.47 (1,019.44 kph) in 1983, said the ultimate aim of the desert trials next month was to prepare the car to break the sound barrier in 1997.
"We want to get the car well over 600 miles an hour (960 kph) to find out what's going to happen to it...in preparation for the supersonic attempt next year," Green said.
Noble said he was confident the 16 metre, 9.5 tonne car was up to the challenge.

"This is a very original and revolutionary machine... It's got two jet engines -- nobody's ever built a car like that before," he said, pointing to twin jets from a Phantom warplane which straddle the driver's cockpit.
The British team is racing to break the sound barrier ahead of long-time rival American Craig Breedlove, currently testing his car, the Spirit of America, in Nevada's Black Rock Desert.

Noble said the arid climate in southern Jordan may give the Thrust team an edge over the American, struggling with rain in Nevada. But an additional challenge from an Australian team could turn the rivalry into a three-way race, he added.

Thrust SSC, designed to reach 850 mph (1,360 kph), is not expected to get close to that speed because the mud flats at Jafr are just 10 miles long -- about two thirds of the distance needed for the car to reach supersonic speeds.

Organiser Andrew Noble, Richard's younger brother, said the car was expected to make its first outing on Wednesday or Thursday. It will start at around 200 mph (320 kph) and build up around 100 mph per day.
"We're not going crazy first time out and trying to go 600 mph," Noble told reporters earlier on Saturday on the dried out mud basin where the test runs will take place.
Seventeen thick white lines, 50 feet apart and 10 miles long, have been drawn along the desert floor, giving Jafr the appearance of a giants' athletics track.
The car will drive along each line just once, because its 34 inch (86 cm) diameter aluminium wheels will bite deep ruts into the ground.

Andrew Noble said the site at Jafr, with its "fantastic" driving surface, only came to the team's attention last year, when a retired British soldier told them how he had driven an army truck across its featureless landscape 50 years ago.
After smoothing over two areas marked by bedouin tracks and removing a few stones, the track was ready.
"All that's left now is a little camel dung," said Noble. "I don't think that should be a problem."
